Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Hillary Clinton was sworn in as the 67th U.S. secretary of state Wednesday afternoon after the Senate approved her nomination by a vote of 94-2. Hillary Clinton gets sworn in Wednesday in her Senate office by Judge Kathryn Oberly. Former President Clinton and her Senate staff looked on as Clinton's childhood friend and D.C. Court of Appeals Associate Judge Kathryn Oberly swore her in on a Bible belonging to the former first lady's late father in a ceremony in her Senate office. The senators who opposed Clinton's confirmation were Jim DeMint, R-South Carolina, and David Vitter, R-Louisiana. Keeping with tradition, America's new chief diplomat will be treated to a welcoming ceremony with employees Thursday morning in the State Department, agency officials said. Immediately after the ceremony, Clinton submitted her resignation from the Senate with identical one-sentence letters to Vice President Joe Biden, who serves as president of the Senate, Secretary of the Senate Nancy Erickson and New York Gov. David Paterson. Paterson must appoint a replacement in the Senate. The governor, who had said he would not name his choice until after Clinton's confirmation, told CNN's "American Morning" on Monday that he had not made a decision. "I'm actually, I think, narrowing the field to about half of the people who are involved, and then I would hope, in the next few days, to get down to one," he told CNN's John Roberts. Some of the better-known candidates, including Nassau County Executive Tom Suozzi and U.S. Reps. Carolyn Maloney and Steve Israel, have pledged not to wage a primary fight against Paterson's pick in the 2010 special election to finish the final two years of Clinton's term. Clinton's confirmation was held up Tuesday when Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn objected to a voice vote, demanding a roll-call vote instead. Cornyn said he knew that Clinton would be confirmed but said he delayed the vote because he wanted more time to talk about the foundation run by her husband. The former president signed an agreement with the Obama transition team pledging to limit foreign donations and to release annual disclosures of new donations to his foundation. "My concern is not whether our colleague Sen. Clinton is qualified to be secretary of state or not. She is," Cornyn said. "But we should not let our respect for Sen. Clinton or our admiration for the many good works of the Clinton Foundation blind us to the danger of perceived conflicts of interest caused by the [foundation's] solicitation of hundreds of millions of dollars from foreign and some domestic sources," he said. "The perception and reality must be that the office of secretary of state is viewed around the world as beyond reproach." Clinton was defended by Sen. John McCain, R-Arizona, who used his first floor speech since the end of the presidential campaign to urge his colleagues to confirm her quickly as secretary of state. iReport.com: Share your thoughts on Obama's cabinet . "I think the message that the American people are sending us now is they want us to work together and get to work," McCain said. "I think we ought to let Sen. Clinton, who is obviously qualified and obviously will serve, get to work immediately." McCain confidantes told CNN that the senator developed a genuinely deep admiration for Clinton during the drawn-out Democratic primary process. Both senators also sit on the Armed Services Committee and had become close on several congressional delegation trips abroad. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee voted 16-1 last week in favor of Clinton's nomination, with Vitter casting the sole dissenting vote. CNN's Dana Bash, Ed Hornick and Elise Labott contributed to this report.

Clinton’s childhood friend, D.C. Court of Appeals Associate Judge Kathryn Oberly, administered the oath in Clinton’s Senate office as former President Clinton and members of her Senate staff looked on. Clinton was sworn in using a Bible that belonged to the former first lady’s late father.

Some of the better-known candidates—including Nassau County Executive Tom Suozzi and U.S. Reps. Carolyn Maloney and Steve Israel—have pledged not to mount a primary challenge against Paterson’s appointee in the 2010 special election to complete the final two years of Clinton’s term.

Clinton’s confirmation was delayed Tuesday when Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, objected to a voice vote and demanded a roll-call vote instead.

Cornyn said he knew Clinton would be confirmed but delayed the vote because he wanted more time to discuss the foundation run by her husband.

The former president signed an agreement with the Obama transition team pledging to limit foreign donations and release annual disclosures of new contributions to his foundation.

“My concern is not whether our colleague Sen. Clinton is qualified to be secretary of state or not. She is,” Cornyn said.

“But we should not let our respect for Sen. Clinton or our admiration for the many good works of the Clinton Foundation blind us to the danger of perceived conflicts of interest caused by the [foundation’s] solicitation of hundreds of millions of dollars from foreign and some domestic sources,” he said. “The perception and reality must be that the office of secretary of state is viewed around the world as beyond reproach.”

outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — Following a 94-2 Senate confirmation vote, Hillary Clinton took office Wednesday afternoon as the nation’s 67th secretary of state.

The private swearing-in took place in Clinton’s Senate office. Kathryn Oberly, a childhood friend of Clinton’s and an associate judge on the D.C. Court of Appeals, administered the oath using a Bible that had belonged to Clinton’s late father. Former President Bill Clinton and members of her Senate staff attended the ceremony.

The only senators voting against her confirmation were Republicans Jim DeMint of South Carolina and David Vitter of Louisiana.

State Department officials said the department would follow customary practice by holding a Thursday morning welcome ceremony for Clinton with agency employees.

As soon as the swearing-in ended, Clinton formally left the Senate. She sent matching, single-sentence resignation letters to Vice President Joe Biden in his role as Senate president, Senate Secretary Nancy Erickson, and New York Gov. David Paterson.

Paterson is responsible for selecting someone to fill Clinton’s vacant seat. He had said he would wait until she was confirmed before announcing his choice. Appearing Monday on CNN’s “American Morning,” the governor told John Roberts that he still had not decided. Paterson said he believed he was reducing the candidate pool to roughly half of those under consideration and hoped to settle on one person within several days.

Several prominent possible appointees—including Nassau County Executive Tom Suozzi and U.S. Representatives Carolyn Maloney and Steve Israel—said they would not challenge Paterson’s selection in a primary during the 2010 special election. That contest would determine who serves the final two years of Clinton’s Senate term.

The confirmation process was delayed Tuesday after Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas blocked approval by voice vote and insisted that senators vote individually on the record. Cornyn acknowledged that Clinton would ultimately win confirmation, but said the postponement was intended to allow more discussion of the foundation operated by her husband.

Former President Clinton had reached an agreement with President Obama’s transition team under which he promised to restrict overseas contributions and provide yearly public reports listing new donations to the foundation.

Cornyn emphasized that he did not question Clinton’s qualifications, saying she was capable of serving as secretary of state. His concern, he explained, was that respect for Clinton and praise for the Clinton Foundation’s charitable work should not obscure the potential appearance of conflicts created by the organization’s efforts to raise hundreds of millions of dollars from foreign and domestic donors. He argued that both in fact and in public perception, the secretary of state’s office must be regarded worldwide as above suspicion.

Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain came to Clinton’s defense. In his first Senate floor address since the presidential campaign ended, he called on fellow lawmakers to approve her nomination without delay. McCain said voters wanted Washington officials to cooperate and begin working, and he argued that Clinton was clearly qualified, certain to be confirmed, and should be allowed to start immediately.

People close to McCain told CNN that he had developed sincere and substantial respect for Clinton during the lengthy Democratic presidential primary. The two senators also served together on the Armed Services Committee and had grown close while participating in several congressional trips overseas.

A week earlier, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee had endorsed Clinton’s nomination by a 16-1 margin. Vitter cast the committee’s only opposing vote.

iReport.com invited readers to offer their views on Obama’s Cabinet.

CNN’s Dana Bash, Ed Hornick, and Elise Labott contributed to the report.

WASHINGTON — The Senate confirmed Hillary Rodham Clinton as the nation’s 67th secretary of state on January 21, 2009, approving her nomination by an overwhelming 94-2 roll-call vote.

Shortly after the vote, Clinton was sworn in during a ceremony in her Senate office by Judge Kathryn Oberly of the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. Her husband, former President Bill Clinton, and members of her staff attended as she took the oath and formally joined President Barack Obama’s administration.

Only Republican Senators Jim DeMint of South Carolina and David Vitter of Louisiana voted against her confirmation. The vote had been delayed briefly amid questions about foreign donations to the charitable foundation established by former President Clinton and whether those contributions could create conflicts of interest. Hillary Clinton pledged to follow disclosure and ethics agreements intended to address those concerns.

Following her confirmation, Clinton resigned the New York Senate seat she had held since 2001. Her departure required New York Governor David Paterson to appoint a successor to serve until a special election could be held.

As secretary of state, Clinton became the administration’s chief diplomat and one of its most prominent foreign-policy officials. She assumed responsibility for representing the United States abroad, managing the State Department and helping shape the new administration’s approach to international challenges.
